items.title: Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist?
items.summary: Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron , CTO of Thomson Reuters , about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems. Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Why Thomson Reuters decided to build its own AI model From basic fine-tuning to a comprehensive training pipeline Starting with Qwen and adapting to new open-weight models The economics of building a frontier model: $450K versus $40 million Building the team and harnessing expertise from 3,000 domain experts Model realignment, constitutional principles, and trust Preparing proprietary data, selective pre-training, and agentic tools Training infrastructure, reinforcement learning, and agentic RL Inside CoCounsel: Model orchestration, routing, and production usage Swapping foundation models, deploying smaller models, and reducing third-party reliance AI for tax preparation: Verification, interpretation, and human judgment Continual learning, data privacy, and the roadmap for Thomson AI in legal work: Capabilities, verification, human oversight, and training junior lawyers The future of open-weight models, frontier labs, and enterprise AI Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI.


Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron, CTO of Thomson Reuters, about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems.

      3. Starting with Qwen and adapting to new open-weight models
      4. The economics of building a frontier model: $450K versus $40 million
      5. Building the team and harnessing expertise from 3,000 domain experts

items.title: What Shared Intelligence Really Fixes in Enterprise AI - with John McMullan of Observe.ai
items.summary: Enterprise CX teams have poured budget into AI, yet many still can't show measurable returns — frontline staff double-check the tools, and each new bot becomes another disconnected silo. ​ In this episode, John McMullan, Head of Product Marketing and Strategy at Observe.AI, joins host Yolandi de Weerdt to examine why AI adopted without operational discipline falls short, and how a shared interaction intelligence layer can carry context across AI agents, core systems, and human handoffs. ​ McMullan outlines the practical shifts: putting frontline experts, analysts, and engineers on the build team, starting with one small workflow and learning from early failures, testing agents against simulations of real conversations, and getting data clean and connected before scaling.
